newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge revises controversial bankruptcy order.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge revises controversial bankruptcy order.

text.p: A federal judge Friday said he would take charge of managing the assignment and handling of bankruptcy cases in one of the major U.S. venues for deciding corporate bankruptcies.

In an order clarifying a controversial decision last week, Chief Judge Joseph Farnan of the U.S. District Court of Delaware said that, starting Monday, he would be in charge of assigning all new Chapter 11 bankruptcy regoranization cases and would assign them to any of the two bankruptcy judges in the district and three regular district judges.

This responsibility was previously that of the district's chief bankruptcy Judge Helen Balick, who, according to Friday's order will continue to oversee the hundreds of cases already in progress and Chapter 7 liqudation cases.

The Delaware courts are a major forum for U.S. corporate bankruptcies because of the many companies incorporated in the state and Farnan's recent involvement in the bankruptcy courts has sparked consternation among U.S. bankruptcy attorneys and the companies they represent.

A legal source told Reuters potential corporate clients had grown uneasy about the uncertainties of having their cases tried by judges without a bankruptcy track record. The source said two potential clients of one of Delaware's major bankruptcy law firms have already decided to go elsewhere.
"They said when the time came they would probably file in the Southern District of New York instead," the source said, speaking on condition that he not be identified.
District Court spokesman Peter Dalleo told Reuters Farnan's decision to begin assigning chapter 11 cases himself was triggered by the bankruptcy court's heavy caseload.
In response to numerous queries from companies and attorneys, Farnan has convened an advisory committee of nine bankruptcy lawyers to monitor implementation of the new order.
He reassured committee members at the initial meeting Wednesday that the district judges could handle bankruptcy cases efficiently.

Committee co-chairman William Sudell told Reuters Farnam's decision to become involved in the handling of bankruptcy cases did not reflect an opinion regarding the skills of the current bankruptcy judges.

"Judge Farnan has nothing but admiration for the job Judges Balick and (Bankruptcy Judge) Peter Walsh are doing...The reason for the order comes out of the fact that over the last six to seven years the number of bankruptcy cases has grown," Sudell said.

According to a records released Friday , the Delaware bankruptcy court has since 1990 had more than five hundred chapter 11 cases involving assets of more than a million dollars. That figure includes 24 companies with assets or liabilities of more than $1 billion and 62 companies with cases of $100 million or more.
